title: Particulate Nature of Matter
subject: Science
description: Grade 8 practice on constituent particles, interparticle attraction and spacing, the solid, liquid and gaseous states, melting and boiling, compressibility, particle motion and the chapter's exercises.

questions.question: According to the chapter, where do the pebbles, stones and sand found on a riverbank mainly come from?
options: Rocks in mountains broken down by erosion and carried along by rivers
Shells of sea creatures crushed slowly by the waves of the ocean
Volcanic ash that settled on the plains and hardened over many years
Soil washed off farms into rivers during the heavy monsoon rains
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that rocks in the mountains break down due to erosion; rivers carry the pieces and keep breaking them into pebbles, stones and sand, transporting them to the plains.

questions.question: In Activity 7.1, chalk is broken, ground with a mortar and pestle, and the powder is viewed with a magnifying glass. What does each tiny grain turn out to be?
options: A grain of stone from the mortar
Still a speck of the same chalk
A new white substance called lime
A mixture of chalk and fine dust
questions.explanation: Grinding only reduces the size of each speck; every grain observed is still chalk. No new substance is formed, so it is a physical change.

questions.question: Grinding chalk into fine powder is classified as a physical change because
options: the chalk powder can no longer be pressed back together
the colour of the chalk becomes lighter as it is powdered
only the size of each speck is reduced, not the substance
heat is released as the pestle rubs against the chalk
questions.explanation: Recalling Grade 7, the chapter states chalk does not change into a new substance on grinding; only the size of each speck reduces, which is the mark of a physical change.

questions.question: What does the chapter call the basic unit that makes up a larger piece of a substance or material?
options: Suspended particle
Interparticle space
Compound particle
Constituent particle
questions.explanation: A constituent particle is defined as the basic unit that makes up a larger piece of a substance. 'Suspended particulate matter' refers to dust in air, a different idea.

questions.question: A grain of sand is the smallest possible unit of a rock and cannot be broken down any further.
questions.explanation: The chapter says grains of sand and clay are NOT the smallest units of rocks; like chalk, they are made up of a large number of constituent particles.

questions.question: In Activity 7.2, water from the top layer is not sweet before stirring but is sweet after the sugar dissolves. What does the sweet taste after stirring prove?
options: Sugar is still present in the solution even though it cannot be seen
Sugar has changed into a new substance that tastes much sweeter
Stirring pushes all of the sugar up into the top layer of the water
The water itself turns sweet when it is stirred for long enough
questions.explanation: The sugar particles can no longer be observed, but their presence is sensed by taste — so sugar is still there, broken into constituent particles spread through the water.

questions.question: When sugar dissolves, it 'breaks up into its constituent particles'. How many such particles does the chapter say make up one tiny grain of sugar?
options: Just one large particle
Millions and millions
Exactly two particles
A few hundred particles
questions.explanation: The text says each tiny grain of sugar is made up of millions and millions of constituent particles, which cannot be broken down further.

questions.question: Which statement about the particles of matter is NOT supported by Activities 7.1 and 7.2?
options: They are extremely small, far beyond ordinary sight
Dissolved sugar exists in water as such particles
They are visible under an ordinary microscope
Matter is composed of a very large number of them
questions.explanation: The chapter says these particles are so small that they cannot be seen even through an ordinary microscope. The other three statements are exactly what the activities support.

questions.question: The spaces between the particles of matter are known as
options: interparticle forces
constituent gaps
particle vacuums
interparticle spaces
questions.explanation: The chapter names the spaces between particles 'interparticle spaces'; interparticle forces are the attractions that act across those spaces.

questions.question: After sugar dissolves in water, where do the tiny sugar particles go?
options: Into the spaces between the water particles
To the bottom, forming an invisible layer
Into the air above the water as vapour
Onto the inner walls of the glass tumbler
questions.explanation: The sugar particles separate and occupy the available interparticle spaces between water particles — which is why the top layer tastes sweet too.

questions.question: Activities 7.1 and 7.2 support the idea that matter is composed of a large number of extremely small particles.
questions.explanation: Both the chalk-grinding and sugar-dissolving activities lead to the conclusion that matter is made of a very large number of extremely small particles.

questions.question: Which of these does the chapter describe as being made up of a large number of constituent particles? (Select all that apply)
options: A grain of sand
A speck of chalk powder
The space between water particles
The sweet taste of sugar
questions.explanation: Sand grains and chalk specks are both made of many constituent particles. Interparticle space is empty space, and taste is a sensation, not a piece of matter.

questions.question: A student claims that if chalk were ground for long enough, the final particles would no longer be chalk. Based on the chapter, the correct response is:
options: Grinding is a chemical change because the pieces look different
Grinding finally gives the constituent particles that chalk is built from
Grinding changes chalk into lime once the specks become very small
Grinding stops being a physical change after the powder stage
questions.explanation: Imagining the grinding continued, the chapter says we reach units that cannot be broken further — the constituent particles the chalk was made of. The substance never changes.

questions.question: The 'Safety first' note for the sugar-tasting activity says you should
options: use warm water so the sugar dissolves faster
wear gloves while handling the sugar spoon
taste only when asked, under adult supervision
stir the sugar quickly to avoid any spilling
questions.explanation: The note says to perform the activity under the supervision of a teacher or adult and never eat or drink anything unless asked to.

questions.question: The forces that hold the constituent particles of matter together are called
options: gravitational attractions
frictional resistances
magnetic attractions
interparticle attractions
questions.explanation: The chapter names the attractive forces between constituent particles 'interparticle attractions'.

questions.question: The interparticle forces described in the chapter are
options: attractive in nature
repulsive in nature
neutral in nature
electrical in nature
questions.explanation: The text states that constituent particles are held together through forces which are attractive in nature.

questions.question: According to the chapter, the strength of interparticle attraction depends on which factors? (Select all that apply)
options: The nature of the substance
The interparticle distance
The colour of the substance
The size of the container
questions.explanation: The chapter says the strength of these attractions depends on the nature of the substance and on the interparticle distance. Colour and container size are irrelevant.

questions.question: What happens to the interparticle forces when the distance between particles increases even slightly?
options: They become repulsive
They decrease drastically
They increase slightly
They remain unchanged
questions.explanation: The chapter stresses that even a slight increase in interparticle distance decreases the interparticle forces drastically.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what ultimately decides the physical state of a substance?
options: The colour and hardness of the material
The shape of the container it is kept in
The strength of the interparticle forces
The mass of the individual particles
questions.explanation: The text says the strength of the interparticle forces ultimately decides the physical state of the substance.

questions.question: A small increase in interparticle distance causes only a small decrease in the interparticle forces of attraction.
questions.explanation: The chapter says the opposite: even a slight increase in distance decreases the interparticle forces drastically.

questions.question: Two substances have the same interparticle distance, yet one is a solid and the other a liquid at room temperature. Which chapter idea best explains this?
options: Interparticle attraction depends only on the interparticle distance
The solid must have particles far larger than those of the liquid
The liquid must contain air trapped inside its interparticle spaces
Interparticle attraction also depends on the nature of the substance
questions.explanation: Strength of attraction depends on two things — distance AND the nature of the substance. With equal distances, the difference in nature explains the different states.

questions.question: The ancient Indian philosopher who first spoke about the idea of Parmanu (atom) was
options: Kanad
Aryabhata
Charaka
Sushruta
questions.explanation: Acharya Kanad first spoke about Parmanu — tiny, indivisible, eternal particles of matter. Aryabhata, Charaka and Sushruta are known for astronomy and medicine.

questions.question: Kanad's idea about Parmanu was written in his work called the
options: Surya Siddhanta
Vaisheshika Sutras
Charaka Samhita
Brahmasphuta Siddhanta
questions.explanation: The chapter's 'Our scientific heritage' box says Kanad's idea of Parmanu was written in the Vaisheshika Sutras.

questions.question: Kanad believed that matter is made up of tiny, indivisible and eternal particles called Parmanu.
questions.explanation: This is exactly how the chapter describes Kanad's view of matter in the 'Our scientific heritage' box.

questions.question: In the chapter's final summary, the distance between particles is said to depend on their
options: mass and their density
chemical composition
thermal (heat) energy
electrical charge
questions.explanation: The summary says attraction depends on interparticle distance, which in turn depends on the thermal (heat) energy of the particles.

questions.question: Which statement about interparticle attraction is NOT correct?
options: It is strongest in solids and weakest in gases
It becomes weaker as particles move farther apart
It depends on the nature of the substance
It is strongest in gases and weakest in solids
questions.explanation: The Snapshots say attraction is strongest in solids, a little weaker in liquids and weakest in gases — the first option reverses this.

questions.question: Which chain of reasoning correctly follows the chapter?
options: Higher thermal energy → larger interparticle distance → weaker attraction
Higher thermal energy → smaller interparticle distance → weaker attraction
Lower thermal energy → larger interparticle distance → stronger attraction
Lower thermal energy → smaller interparticle distance → weaker attraction
questions.explanation: More thermal energy lets particles move farther apart, and attraction falls as distance grows. The other chains pair distance and attraction the wrong way round.

questions.question: Solids have a definite shape and volume mainly because
options: their interparticle spaces are completely filled with air
their particles are tightly packed with very strong attractions
their particles are far apart with negligible attractions
their particles move freely but only within a limited space
questions.explanation: In solids the particles are tightly packed and interparticle attractions are very strong, holding particles in fixed positions — hence definite shape and volume.

questions.question: Particles in a solid can
options: move anywhere in the container
escape easily into the open air
only vibrate about fixed positions
slide freely past one another
questions.explanation: Strong forces hold solid particles in fixed positions; they can only move to and fro (vibrate or oscillate) about those positions and cannot move past each other.

questions.question: In a solid, strong forces of attraction hold the particles in fixed positions, but the particles can still slide past each other.
questions.explanation: Solid particles only vibrate about their positions; the chapter says they cannot move past each other. Moving past each other is a liquid property.

questions.question: Which of these objects were listed for study in Activity 7.3? (Select all that apply)
options: Iron nail
Rock salt
Glass of water
Candle wax
Rubber band
questions.explanation: Activity 7.3 lists an iron nail, rock salt, a stone, a piece of wood, a key and a piece of aluminium — all solids. Water is a liquid; wax and rubber are not listed.

questions.question: Despite close packing, what fills the small spaces left between the particles of a solid?
options: Only trapped air
Water vapour
Tiny dust grains
Nothing at all
questions.explanation: The chapter warns that you might assume the spaces are filled with air, but they contain nothing at all.

questions.question: A student says the gaps between particles in a solid must contain air because 'something has to be there'. The chapter's view is that
options: the gaps contain nothing at all
the gaps hold a thin layer of air
the gaps contain water vapour
the gaps are filled with heat
questions.explanation: The text directly addresses this misconception: the interparticle spaces in solids are not filled with air; they contain nothing.

questions.question: Which property distinguishes solids from fluids (liquids and gases)?
options: Solids are made of particles and fluids are not
Solids retain a fixed shape and do not flow
Solids have a definite volume and fluids do not
Solids have interparticle spaces and fluids do not
questions.explanation: Liquids and gases flow and do not retain a fixed shape; these properties classify them as fluids and distinguish them from solids. Liquids also have a definite volume.

questions.question: You can move your finger through water but not through a block of wood. In the wood this is because
options: there are no interparticle spaces at all in the wood
particles are moving too fast to be displaced
particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces
particles are too large for the finger to push aside
questions.explanation: Strong interparticle attractions hold a solid's particles in fixed positions, so they cannot be displaced the way water particles are.

questions.question: Rock salt, an iron nail and a wooden block all have a definite shape and a definite volume.
questions.explanation: All these objects in Activity 7.3 are solids, and the chapter says solids have a definite shape and volume.

questions.question: Which statement about solids is NOT correct?
options: Their particles only vibrate about fixed positions
Their interparticle attractions are the strongest
They have a fixed shape and a fixed volume
Their particles have no interparticle spaces
questions.explanation: Even in closely packed solids, some space is left between particles (Fig. 7.12a) — it is minimum, not zero.

questions.question: In the 'Let us wrap up' table, the movement of particles in solids is described as
options: negligible (only vibrations)
restricted to a limited space
free in all available space
fast but in one direction
questions.explanation: The table lists solid particle movement as negligible (only vibrations); 'restricted to limited space' is for liquids and 'all available space' is for gases.

questions.question: Hammering the solid objects in Activity 7.3 helps a student judge
options: how fast the particles of each solid are vibrating
how strongly particles are held together in each solid
which of the solids has the lowest melting point
which solid contains the most interparticle space
questions.explanation: The activity asks in which objects the particles are strongly held together; hammering tests how firmly the solid resists being deformed or broken.

questions.question: In the wrap-up table, the interparticle spacing in solids is
options: moderate
variable
minimum
maximum
questions.explanation: Solids have minimum interparticle spacing; liquids have a little more and gases have the maximum.

questions.question: What happens to the particles of a solid when it is heated?
options: They stop vibrating completely
They shrink to a smaller size
They become noticeably heavier
They vibrate more vigorously
questions.explanation: Heating makes solid particles vibrate more vigorously (Fig. 7.4b) until they start leaving their positions.

questions.question: The temperature at which vibrations become so vigorous that particles leave their positions and the solid turns into a liquid is called the
options: melting point
boiling point
freezing level
vapour point
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's description of melting; the temperature at which it happens is the melting point. Boiling point is the liquid-to-vapour change.

questions.question: The chapter defines the melting point as the minimum temperature at which a solid melts into a liquid at
options: any given pressure
atmospheric pressure
very high pressure
very low pressure
questions.explanation: Both melting point and boiling point are defined in the chapter at atmospheric pressure.

questions.question: From Table 7.1, the melting point of urea is
questions.explanation: Table 7.1 lists ice 0 °C, urea 133 °C and iron 1538 °C.

questions.question: From Table 7.1, which material has the highest melting point?
options: Urea
Ice
Chalk
Iron
questions.explanation: Iron melts at 1538 °C, far above urea (133 °C) and ice (0 °C). Chalk is not in the table.

questions.question: Iron melts at 1538 °C while urea melts at 133 °C. According to the chapter, this tells us that
options: iron has stronger interparticle attractions than urea
iron particles are farther apart than urea particles
urea has stronger interparticle attractions than iron
urea particles vibrate less than iron particles on heating
questions.explanation: Solids with weak interparticle forces have low melting points; those with strong attractive forces have high melting points. Iron's high value means stronger attraction.

questions.question: In every substance, the particles in the liquid state are farther apart than in the solid state.
questions.explanation: This is generally true, but the chapter gives ice as an exception — its particles are farther apart than those in liquid water.

questions.question: Which substance is named in the chapter as an exception where particles in the solid are farther apart than in the liquid?
options: Rock salt
Ice (water)
Iron metal
Solid urea
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that ice is an exception: its particles are farther apart than those in liquid water.

questions.question: Why do some solids have low melting points?
options: Their interparticle spaces are filled with air
Their particles already move freely at room temperature
Their interparticle forces of attraction are weak
Their particles are larger than those of other solids
questions.explanation: The chapter links weak interparticle attraction to low melting points and strong attraction to high melting points.

questions.question: Solid X melts at 50 °C and solid Y melts at 800 °C. Which statement is correct?
options: X's particles are held by stronger attractions than Y's
X must have far smaller interparticle spaces than Y's
Y must already be a fluid at room temperature
Y's particles need more energy to leave their positions
questions.explanation: A higher melting point means stronger attraction, so more thermal energy is needed to overcome it. X has the weaker attraction, and both are solids at room temperature.

questions.question: Ice melts at
questions.explanation: Table 7.1 gives the melting point of ice as 0 °C; 133 °C is urea and 1538 °C is iron.

questions.question: At the melting point, the thermal energy supplied is used to
options: fill the interparticle spaces with heat
overcome the attractive forces between particles
increase the size of each constituent particle
break the particles into smaller particles
questions.explanation: The summary says that at the melting point thermal energy is used to overcome the attractive forces, allowing the solid to become a liquid.

questions.question: When a solid melts, the interparticle forces of attraction get weakened.
questions.explanation: The chapter says vibrations become so vigorous that particles leave their positions, the interparticle forces weaken, and the solid becomes a liquid.

questions.question: Fig. 7.4 shows (a) a solid, (b) particles with increased vibrations and (c) a liquid. The correct cause→effect sequence from (a) to (c) is
options: cooling → stronger vibrations → particles leave positions → liquid
heating → stronger vibrations → particles break apart → liquid
heating → stronger vibrations → particles leave positions → liquid
heating → weaker vibrations → particles lock in place → liquid
questions.explanation: Heating increases vibration until particles leave their positions and attraction weakens. The particles themselves do not break apart; they just move more freely.

questions.question: Which statements about the melting points in Table 7.1 are correct? (Select all that apply)
options: Iron melts at 1538 °C
Urea melts at 133 °C
Ice melts at 100 °C
Urea has the highest melting point of the three
questions.explanation: Table 7.1: ice 0 °C, urea 133 °C, iron 1538 °C. Ice does not melt at 100 °C, and iron, not urea, has the highest melting point.

questions.question: In Activity 7.4, when 200 mL of water is poured from Container A to B and then to C, the water
options: keeps its shape but changes its volume
changes both its shape and its volume
keeps both its shape and its volume
changes shape but stays at the 200 mL level
questions.explanation: The water takes the shape of each container, but its level stays at 200 mL — liquids have no fixed shape but a definite volume.

questions.question: Liquids take the shape of their container because
options: their particles are free to move
their particles are fixed in position
they have no interparticle attraction
their particles are very far apart
questions.explanation: Liquid particles can move (within a limited space), so the liquid flows to take the container's shape. Liquids still have attraction and are not far apart like gases.

questions.question: Activity 7.4 shows that particles of liquids can move freely but
options: only at the surface of the liquid
only within a limited space
only in a single direction
only when the liquid is heated
questions.explanation: The chapter infers that liquid particles move freely but only within a limited space — which is why volume stays fixed while shape changes.

questions.question: In Activity 7.4, a student finds the level in Container C slightly below 200 mL. According to the chapter, the most likely reason is
options: some water escaped into the interparticle spaces of the glass
liquids slowly lose volume each time they change their shape
some water stuck to the walls of a container that was not clean
the water particles shrank as they moved to a new container
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that if a container is not clean, some water sticks to its walls, so the level in the next container may be slightly less than 200 mL.

questions.question: Liquids have a fixed volume but no fixed shape.
questions.explanation: This is the conclusion of Activity 7.4: volume stays at 200 mL while shape changes with the container.

questions.question: Why can you move your finger through water without permanently cutting it?
options: Water particles are broken apart and quickly join again as new particles
Water has no interparticle attraction so nothing resists the finger
Water particles are too small to be noticed when they are pushed
Water is only temporarily displaced and returns when the finger is removed
questions.explanation: The finger temporarily displaces water; as soon as it is removed, the water's position is restored. Attraction in liquids is weaker than in solids but still present.

questions.question: Compared to solids, interparticle attractions in liquids are
options: slightly weaker, yet enough to keep particles close
negligible, allowing particles to move anywhere
much stronger, holding particles in fixed positions
equal in strength but acting in different directions
questions.explanation: The chapter says attractions in liquids are slightly weaker than in solids but strong enough to keep particles close together. Negligible attraction describes gases.

questions.question: In the wrap-up table, the movement of particles in liquids is
options: completely absent at all times
restricted to a limited space
negligible (only vibrations)
in all the available space
questions.explanation: Liquid particle movement is restricted to a limited space; 'only vibrations' is solids and 'all available space' is gases.

questions.question: Which statement about liquids is NOT correct?
options: They have a definite, fixed volume
Their particles can move past one another
They have no interparticle spaces at all
They take the shape of their container
questions.explanation: Liquids do have interparticle spaces — a little more than solids — which is where dissolved sugar particles go. The other statements are correct.

questions.question: In the wrap-up table, interparticle spacing in liquids is described as
options: exactly equal to that in solids
far greater than in gases
the maximum of all three
a little more than in solids
questions.explanation: The table says liquid spacing is a little more than in solids; gases have the maximum.

questions.question: Because liquid particles can move freely, liquids have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume.
questions.explanation: Liquid particles move only within a limited space, so liquids have no fixed shape but DO have a fixed volume. Having neither is a property of gases.

questions.question: The chapter infers that liquids have a fixed volume because
options: the water level stayed at 200 mL in all three containers
the water took the shape of each of the containers
the water could be displaced by moving a finger
the water felt the same temperature in each container
questions.explanation: No change in volume was observed as the water moved between containers, which shows a definite volume. Taking the container's shape shows the lack of fixed shape.

questions.question: Which properties does the chapter use to classify liquids and gases together as fluids? (Select all that apply)
options: They flow
They do not retain a fixed shape
They have a fixed volume
They are incompressible
questions.explanation: Both liquids and gases flow and do not retain a fixed shape — these two properties classify them as fluids. Gases have no fixed volume and are compressible.

questions.question: Which observations were made in Activity 7.4? (Select all that apply)
options: Water took the shape of each container
The water level stayed at the 200 mL mark
Water volume increased in the wider container
Water became colder in each new container
questions.explanation: The two observations were change of shape and constant 200 mL level. Volume did not increase and temperature was not part of the activity.

questions.question: The temperature at which a liquid boils and turns into vapour at atmospheric pressure is its
options: heating point
boiling point
melting point
vapour limit
questions.explanation: This is the chapter's definition of boiling point; melting point refers to a solid becoming a liquid.

questions.question: At the boiling point, vapour forms
options: only within the liquid and never at the surface
only after all of the liquid has become hot
very fast, both at the surface and within the liquid
slowly, only at the surface of the liquid
questions.explanation: At the boiling point vapour formation is very fast and occurs within the liquid as well as at the surface — seen as bubbles. Slow surface-only vapour formation is evaporation.

questions.question: The bubbles seen in boiling water are evidence that
options: air trapped between water particles is escaping
water particles are breaking into smaller particles
interparticle attraction in water is increasing
vapour is forming inside the liquid, not just at the surface
questions.explanation: The chapter says vapour formation within the liquid is observed as bubble formation. Particles do not break into smaller ones; attraction decreases, not increases.

questions.question: Vapour formation that happens slowly, only at the surface, and at all temperatures is called
options: evaporation
boiling
melting
condensation
questions.explanation: Evaporation is the slower process that occurs at all temperatures, even below the boiling point, and only at the surface.

questions.question: A liquid can turn into vapour only when it reaches its boiling point.
questions.explanation: Vapour formation occurs at all temperatures, even below the boiling point, though slowly and only at the surface — this is evaporation.

questions.question: Spilled water on a table disappears after some time even though the room is cool. Which statement explains this?
options: Water particles break down into smaller particles that cannot be seen
Evaporation occurs at all temperatures, slowly and only at the surface
Boiling occurs at all temperatures when the layer of water is thin
Water particles seep into the interparticle spaces of the wooden table
questions.explanation: The chapter's speech bubble notes spilled water disappears at any temperature — evaporation. Boiling needs the boiling point, and particles do not break down further.

questions.question: During boiling, the interparticle forces of attraction in the liquid
options: stay the same but act over a larger area
disappear before any heating happens
decrease as the particles move apart
increase as the particles move faster
questions.explanation: Vigorous movement makes particles move apart, resulting in a decrease in interparticle attraction until particles escape as vapour.

questions.question: Which statements correctly compare boiling and evaporation? (Select all that apply)
options: Boiling happens at a fixed temperature; evaporation at all temperatures
Boiling happens within the liquid too; evaporation only at the surface
Evaporation is faster than boiling
Evaporation happens only above the boiling point
questions.explanation: Boiling occurs at the boiling point, fast, and within the liquid; evaporation is slow, surface-only and happens at all temperatures, including below the boiling point.

questions.question: The chapter recalls observing the temperature of boiling water in which earlier chapter?
options: Grade 7, 'Changes Around Us: Physical and Chemical'
Grade 6, 'Materials Around Us and Their Uses'
Grade 7, 'Heat and Its Effects on Matter'
Grade 6, 'Temperature and Its Measurement'
questions.explanation: The chapter recalls the Grade 6 chapter 'Temperature and Its Measurement'. The Grade 7 'Changes Around Us' chapter is recalled for chalk grinding, not boiling.

questions.question: Eventually, at the boiling point, the constituent particles of a liquid
options: escape from the liquid into the gaseous state
settle down at the bottom of the vessel
stop moving and form a solid layer below
merge together to form larger particles
questions.explanation: The chapter says the constituent particles can escape from the liquid state, converting it into vapour or the gaseous state.

questions.question: At the boiling point, vapour formation occurs not only at the surface but also within the liquid.
questions.explanation: This is why bubbles form inside a boiling liquid, as described in the chapter.

questions.question: Which statement about vapour formation is NOT correct?
options: Boiling produces bubbles of vapour inside the liquid
Evaporation occurs only at the boiling point
Boiling occurs at a fixed temperature at normal pressure
Evaporation takes place only at a liquid's surface
questions.explanation: Evaporation occurs at ALL temperatures, even below the boiling point. The other statements match the chapter.

questions.question: Which of these happen during boiling? (Select all that apply)
options: Bubbles of vapour form inside the liquid
Particles move apart, weakening attraction
Particles come closer together
Vapour forms only at the surface
questions.explanation: At boiling, particles move apart (attraction decreases) and vapour forms within the liquid as bubbles. Surface-only vapour formation describes evaporation.

questions.question: In Activity 7.5, when the glass plate between the two gas jars is removed, the smoke
options: settles down at the bottom of Gas Jar A
rises only up to the top of Gas Jar A
spreads and fills the entire space in Gas Jar B
stays in Gas Jar A because it is heavier than air
questions.explanation: The smoke fills the entire space of Gas Jar B, showing gases have no fixed volume and occupy all available space.

questions.question: The spreading of smoke into the second jar shows that gases
options: have a fixed volume but do not have a fixed shape
have strong attractions between their particles
move only when they are pushed by another gas
have no fixed volume and fill the available space
questions.explanation: Gases tend to occupy the entire available space and acquire the vessel's shape, because their particles move freely with negligible attraction.

questions.question: In Activity 7.5 smoke represents the gaseous state. Why can the motion of gas particles be observed through it?
options: Invisible gas particles constantly hit the tiny suspended smoke particles
Smoke particles are the constituent particles of air made visible
Smoke particles are heavier so they fall and reveal the air currents
Smoke glows faintly when it is hit by the light entering the jar
questions.explanation: The tiny suspended smoke particles are constantly hit by invisible gas particles, and their resulting movement lets us observe the motion of gas particles.

questions.question: Which other substance can be used instead of incense smoke to demonstrate Activity 7.5?
options: Camphor smoke
Iodine vapour
Steam from water
Carbon dioxide
questions.explanation: The chapter says the activity can also be demonstrated using iodine vapour instead of smoke from incense sticks.

questions.question: How is iodine vapour obtained for the demonstration?
options: By burning iodine on a spoon over a candle flame
By grinding iodine to a powder with a mortar and pestle
By keeping solid iodine in a closed gas jar for some time
By dissolving iodine crystals in a little warm water
questions.explanation: Iodine vapour is obtained by placing some solid iodine in a closed gas jar for some time (Fig. 7.8).

questions.question: Interparticle attractions in gases are described in the chapter as
options: very strong
moderate
slightly weak
negligible
questions.explanation: Gas particles move freely in all directions because interparticle attractions are negligible; 'slightly weaker' describes liquids.

questions.question: Gases have no fixed shape but, like liquids, they have a fixed volume.
questions.explanation: Gases have neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume — the smoke spread to fill the second jar. Only liquids combine no fixed shape with a fixed volume.

questions.question: Both liquids and gases are classified as fluids because they
options: flow and do not retain a fixed shape
have a definite volume and flow
can be compressed very easily
have negligible interparticle forces
questions.explanation: Flowing and not retaining a fixed shape are the shared properties that make liquids and gases fluids. Only gases have negligible forces and are easily compressed.

questions.question: Which statement about gases is NOT correct?
options: They spread out to occupy the entire available space
Their particles move only within a limited space
Their particles move freely in all directions
They acquire the shape of the vessel they are in
questions.explanation: 'Within a limited space' is the liquid description. Gas particles move freely in all directions and fill all available space.

questions.question: The safety note in Activity 7.5 warns that vapours of iodine
options: are completely harmless
can crack the glass jar
can cause irritation
are highly explosive
questions.explanation: The 'Safety first' box says to be careful with solid iodine because its vapours can cause irritation.

questions.question: In the wrap-up table, interparticle spacing and interparticle attraction in gases are, respectively,
options: minimum and maximum
maximum and maximum
minimum and minimum
maximum and minimum
questions.explanation: Gases have the maximum interparticle spacing and minimum (negligible) attraction — the reverse of solids.

questions.question: Gases acquire the shape of the vessel they are kept in.
questions.explanation: Like liquids, gases take the shape of their container; unlike liquids they also fill its whole volume.

questions.question: Which of the following are TRUE for the gaseous state? (Select all that apply)
options: Particles move freely in all directions
Interparticle attraction is negligible
Particles are closely packed
The volume is fixed
Particles only vibrate about fixed positions
questions.explanation: Gas particles move freely in all directions with negligible attraction. Close packing and vibration-only motion describe solids; fixed volume describes solids and liquids.

questions.question: Which of these are fluids? (Select all that apply)
options: Water
Iodine vapour
Milk
Rock salt
Iron nail
questions.explanation: Liquids (water, milk) and gases (iodine vapour) flow and have no fixed shape, so they are fluids. Rock salt and an iron nail are solids.

questions.question: In Activity 7.6, when the plunger of a sealed syringe full of air is pushed inward, the volume of air
options: decreases
increases
stays constant
first rises, then falls
questions.explanation: With the thumb sealing the open end, pushing the plunger compresses the air and its volume decreases.

questions.question: Air in the syringe can be compressed because
options: gas particles escape through the syringe wall
gas particles have a lot of space between them
gas particles are tightly packed together
gas particles become smaller under pressure
questions.explanation: Gas particles have a lot of space between them in their natural state, which external pressure can reduce by forcing them closer.

questions.question: If you stop pushing the plunger in Activity 7.6, what happens?
options: The plunger keeps moving further inward on its own afterwards
The air inside turns into tiny liquid droplets on the walls
The gas spreads and the plunger returns to its original position
The air stays compressed because the thumb still seals the opening
questions.explanation: The chapter says when you stop pushing, the gas particles spread and the plunger moves back to its original position.

questions.question: When Activity 7.6 is repeated with water instead of air, water is found to be
options: slightly more compressible than air
just as compressible as air
compressible only when it is warm
practically incompressible
questions.explanation: The chapter states that water is practically incompressible, unlike air.

questions.question: Water in a sealed syringe can be compressed to about half its volume by pushing the plunger hard.
questions.explanation: Water is practically incompressible because its particles have far less space between them than gas particles.

questions.question: A student predicts the plunger of a water-filled syringe will move inward as easily as in an air-filled one. Which reasoning corrects this?
options: Liquid particles have far less interparticle space than gas particles
Liquid particles are heavier so they resist the push of the plunger
Water particles are held in fixed positions like those of a solid
Water has no interparticle spaces at all, unlike the air in the syringe
questions.explanation: Compression works by reducing interparticle space. Liquids have only a little more space than solids, so water is practically incompressible — but it does have some space.

questions.question: In Activity 7.7 water is at mark A; sugar is added (mark B) and then dissolved. The new level, mark C, is
options: back down at mark A
slightly below mark B
exactly equal to mark B
clearly above mark B
questions.explanation: The level rises when sugar is added, but after dissolution it may decrease to some extent as sugar particles move into spaces between water particles.

questions.question: The volume of the sugar solution being less than the sum of the volumes of water and sugar shows that
options: some water evaporated while the sugar was being stirred
the sugar particles shrank when they entered the water
there are spaces between water particles which sugar particles occupy
some sugar particles changed into water during the dissolving
questions.explanation: The 'missing' volume shows there is space between water particles, which the dissolved sugar particles occupy (Fig. 7.11).

questions.question: When sand is added to water in Activity 7.7, the total volume
options: decreases, because sand fills interparticle spaces
stays the same, because sand dissolves completely
decreases, because the sand absorbs some water
increases, because sand settles and occupies space
questions.explanation: Sand does not dissolve; its particles settle and occupy space in the container, so the total volume increases.

questions.question: Sugar and sand are both solids. Why does sugar dissolve in water but sand does not?
options: Sand particles are held together too strongly for water particles to pull them out
Sand particles are too large to fit inside the glass vessel with the water
Sugar particles are attracted into the water because sugar is sweet
Sand has no constituent particles, so there is nothing to dissolve
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that in substances like sand, constituent particles are held so strongly that water particles cannot pull them out — hence insoluble.

questions.question: Which substances would behave like sugar (dissolve and occupy interparticle spaces) when Activity 7.7 is repeated? (Select all that apply)
options: Common salt
Glucose
Sand
Stone pieces
questions.explanation: The chapter names common salt and glucose as soluble solids to try, and sand and stone pieces as insoluble ones.

questions.question: Fig. 7.12 shows that interparticle spacing is
options: least in liquids and greatest in solids
least in solids and greatest in gases
least in gases and greatest in solids
equal in all three states of matter
questions.explanation: Fig. 7.12 summarises packing: solids closely packed (least space), liquids a little more, gases the most.

questions.question: Which statement about compressibility is NOT correct?
options: Water is practically incompressible
Compressing a gas forces its particles closer
Liquids can be compressed as easily as gases
Gases can be compressed by external pressure
questions.explanation: Water is practically incompressible, so liquids cannot be compressed like gases. The other three statements match Activity 7.6.

questions.question: Pushing the plunger of a sealed syringe forces the air particles inside to come closer together.
questions.explanation: Compressing the air by pushing the plunger forces the particles closer, reducing the space between them.

questions.question: Which variable is deliberately changed when Activity 7.6 is repeated with water instead of air?
options: The size of the syringe used
The force applied to the plunger
The temperature of the room
The substance inside the syringe
questions.explanation: Only the substance (air → water) is changed, so the difference in compressibility can be attributed to the state of matter inside.

questions.question: A student records: 'Level rose when sugar was added, fell slightly after stirring; with sand it rose and stayed up.' Which conclusion is justified?
options: Sugar particles enter spaces between water particles; sand particles do not
Sand particles enter spaces between water particles; sugar particles do not
Both sugar and sand dissolve, but sand dissolves more slowly
Stirring makes the water particles smaller so the level falls
questions.explanation: The fall after dissolving shows sugar occupying interparticle spaces; the sand level staying up shows sand simply settles and adds its own volume.

questions.question: Which observations show that there are spaces between the particles of matter? (Select all that apply)
options: Air in a syringe gets compressed when the plunger is pushed
Sugar dissolves with only a small rise in the water level
Sand settles and increases the water level
Iron has a very high melting point
questions.explanation: Compression of air and the small volume change on dissolving sugar both reveal interparticle spaces. Sand adding volume and iron's melting point do not show spaces.

questions.question: When a few grains of potassium permanganate are dropped into water, you first see
options: bubbles rising up from the grains
pink streaks spreading out from the grains
the whole water turning pink instantly
the grains floating on the water surface
questions.explanation: Initially, streaks of pink colour spread out from the grain (Fig. 7.13a); only later does the whole water become uniformly pink.

questions.question: After some time the entire water becomes uniformly pink. This happens because
options: the glass tumbler pushes the colour evenly through the water
the permanganate grains dissolve only at the surface of the water
water particles are in constant motion and hit the permanganate particles
potassium permanganate particles sink and then rise again due to heat
questions.explanation: Water particles pull out permanganate particles from the grain and then hit them so they spread throughout the liquid.

questions.question: In Activity 7.8, what do the water particles do FIRST to the potassium permanganate grain?
options: Push the grain down to the bottom
Heat the grain until it melts
Break the grain into smaller grains
Pull out its particles from the grain
questions.explanation: The chapter says water particles first pull out the particles of potassium permanganate from its grain, and later hit them to spread them.

questions.question: The safety note for Activity 7.8 says potassium permanganate should be handled
options: with a spoon or spatula, not with bare hands
only after dissolving it in warm water
with a pair of tongs to avoid burns
while wearing a mask against its vapour
questions.explanation: The 'Safety first' box says do not touch potassium permanganate with your hands; use a spoon or spatula.

questions.question: In the 'Think like a scientist' experiment, potassium permanganate spreads fastest in
options: stirred cold water
hot water
ice-cold water
room-temperature water
questions.explanation: Water particles move fastest in hot water, so the permanganate spreads fastest there, slower at room temperature and slowest in ice-cold water.

questions.question: The permanganate experiment with hot, room-temperature and ice-cold water shows that
options: cold water has more interparticle spaces than hot water
water particles stop moving completely in ice-cold water
the movement of particles increases when heat is provided
potassium permanganate dissolves only in hot water
questions.explanation: The chapter concludes that the movement of particles increases when heat is provided. Permanganate still spreads in cold water, just slowest.

questions.question: In the three-tumbler permanganate experiment, which is the variable being deliberately changed (independent variable)?
options: Amount of potassium permanganate
Size of the glass tumblers
Time taken for colour to spread
Temperature of the water
questions.explanation: Only the water temperature differs between tumblers; the same small grain is dropped in each, and the spreading time is what is observed.

questions.question: In the same experiment, which quantity is observed as the result (dependent variable)?
options: How fast the pink colour spreads
The temperature of the water
The number of grains dropped
The shape of the tumblers
questions.explanation: The speed of spreading of the pink colour is compared across the tumblers; temperature is the variable that was changed.

questions.question: In ice-cold water, water particles stop moving, so potassium permanganate does not spread at all.
questions.explanation: Particles move slower in ice-cold water, not zero; the permanganate still spreads, just the slowest of the three.

questions.question: When an incense stick is lit in one corner of a room, after a few minutes the fragrance
options: disappears completely
is smelt throughout the room
stays only near the stick
sinks down towards the floor
questions.explanation: Initially the fragrance is felt only near the stick, but shortly it can be smelt throughout the room.

questions.question: The spreading of incense fragrance across a room shows that
options: the room's walls reflect the fragrance back and forth
burning converts the fragrance into particles of air
air particles are constantly moving and hit the fragrance particles
fragrance particles are lighter than air and float upward
questions.explanation: The chapter says the particles of air are moving constantly; they hit the fragrance particles and help them spread throughout the room.

questions.question: According to the chapter, why are substances like sand insoluble in water?
options: Their particles are so small that water particles cannot find them
They have no interparticle spaces for the water to enter into
Their particles move too fast to be caught by the water particles
Their particles are held so strongly that water cannot pull them out
questions.explanation: Dissolving needs water particles to pull constituent particles out; in sand they are held too strongly for this to happen.

questions.question: A perfume opened in one corner is smelt across a room after some time, even without a fan. Which chapter idea explains this?
options: Gas particles move constantly and spread into all available space
Perfume particles are pulled along by the attraction of air particles
Perfume evaporates only when the air in the room is completely still
Liquids have no fixed shape, so the perfume spreads along the floor
questions.explanation: Like the incense example, perfume particles in the air are hit by constantly moving air particles and spread through the whole room.

questions.question: Which observations in the chapter demonstrate that particles of matter are in constant motion? (Select all that apply)
options: Potassium permanganate colouring a whole tumbler of water
Incense fragrance reaching every corner of a room
Water keeping a 200 mL volume in different containers
Iron having a very high melting point
questions.explanation: Both the permanganate and incense activities show particles spreading due to constant motion. The constant volume and iron's melting point show other properties.

questions.question: Which statement about particle motion is NOT correct?
options: Moving air particles help fragrance particles spread
Particles in hot water move slower than in cold water
Particles in hot water move faster than in cold water
Water particles are in constant motion at room temperature
questions.explanation: Heat increases particle movement, so hot-water particles move faster — the first statement reverses this.

questions.question: What would you predict if a grain of potassium permanganate is dropped into water that is left completely undisturbed?
options: The grain will remain intact at the bottom forever
The water will turn pink only at the surface
The colour will still spread, only more slowly
The colour will never spread without stirring
questions.explanation: Activity 7.8 involves no stirring — the constant motion of water particles alone spreads the colour until the water is uniformly pink.

questions.question: Which conditions make potassium permanganate spread faster in water? (Select all that apply)
options: Using hot water instead of cold
Water particles moving faster
Using ice-cold water
Water particles being stationary
questions.explanation: Heat makes water particles move faster, which spreads the permanganate faster. Ice-cold water gives the slowest spread, and particles are never stationary.

questions.question: According to the chapter's conclusion, what determines the physical state of matter?
options: The colour of the substance
The size of the container used
The weight of the particles
The particles' thermal energy
questions.explanation: The summary says it is the thermal energy of the particles that determines the physical state, because it controls interparticle distance and hence attraction.

questions.question: In the solid state, the thermal energy of particles is low, so
options: they stay close together with strong attractions and only vibrate
they move freely in all directions with negligible attraction
they move within a limited space with weaker attraction
they escape from the surface into the gaseous state
questions.explanation: Low thermal energy keeps particles close, so they experience strong attraction and their motion is restricted to small vibrations.

questions.question: In the gaseous state, particles have enough energy to
options: come closer together and freeze into a solid
overcome attraction and move freely in all directions
overcome attraction partly and move within a limited space
vibrate vigorously while staying in fixed positions
questions.explanation: Gas particles have enough energy to overcome interparticle attraction and move freely in all directions. Limited-space motion is for liquids.

questions.question: Place the three states in order of increasing interparticle attraction:
options: liquid < gas < solid
gas < solid < liquid
gas < liquid < solid
solid < liquid < gas
questions.explanation: Attraction is minimum (negligible) in gases, slightly weaker than solids in liquids, and maximum in solids.

questions.question: From the Snapshots, interparticle attractions are the strongest in
options: liquids
gases
fluids
solids
questions.explanation: The Snapshots say attractions are strongest in solids, a little weaker in liquids and weakest in gases. Fluids (liquids and gases) have weaker attraction.

questions.question: The interparticle attractions are strongest in solids, a little weaker in liquids, and weakest in gases.
questions.explanation: This is stated directly in the Snapshots.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the melting stage in the chapter's summary?
options: Interparticle distance increases slightly, so attraction falls enough for particles to move within a limited space
Interparticle distance increases greatly, so attraction disappears and particles move anywhere
Interparticle distance decreases, so attraction becomes stronger and particles vibrate less
Interparticle distance stays the same, but particles vibrate faster and escape as vapour
questions.explanation: At melting, distance increases slightly, reducing attraction to a level that lets particles move around within a limited space. Attraction disappearing describes gases.

questions.question: From the wrap-up table, which features belong to the LIQUID state? (Select all that apply)
options: Interparticle spacing a little more than in solids
Movement of particles restricted to a limited space
Interparticle attraction negligible
Particles closely packed with only vibrations
questions.explanation: Liquids: spacing a little more than solids, movement restricted to limited space. Negligible attraction is for gases; close packing with only vibrations is for solids.

questions.question: Which statement is NOT part of the chapter's Snapshots?
options: Gases have neither fixed shape nor fixed volume
Gases have a definite volume but no fixed shape
Matter is composed of extremely small particles
Liquids have a definite volume but no fixed shape
questions.explanation: The Snapshots say gases have no fixed shape AND no fixed volume; a definite volume with no fixed shape is the liquid description.

questions.question: Which pairing of state and interparticle space is correct?
options: Liquid — minimum interparticle space
Gas — minimum interparticle space
Gas — maximum interparticle space
Solid — maximum interparticle space
questions.explanation: Gases have maximum interparticle space, solids minimum, and liquids a little more than solids.

questions.question: In the summary, the strength of the attractive forces depends on the interparticle distance, which in turn depends on the mass of the particles.
questions.explanation: The distance depends on the thermal (heat) energy of the particles, not their mass.

questions.question: A substance's particles move within a limited space, have attraction slightly weaker than in a solid, and spacing a little more than in a solid. Its state is
options: solid
gas
vapour
liquid
questions.explanation: These are exactly the wrap-up table's descriptions of the liquid state. Vapour is a gaseous state with negligible attraction.

questions.question: If the thermal energy of a gas's particles were steadily reduced, which sequence does the chapter's reasoning predict?
options: Particles come closer → attraction increases → gas becomes liquid, then solid
Particles move apart → attraction decreases → gas stays a gas
Particles come closer → attraction decreases → gas becomes a solid
Particles stop moving → attraction disappears → gas becomes a liquid
questions.explanation: Less thermal energy means smaller distance and stronger attraction — reversing the solid→liquid→gas path. Attraction grows, not falls, as particles come closer.

questions.question: The chapter says the particles that constitute matter will be studied further in
options: a laboratory manual
higher grades
the next chapter
the Grade 6 book
questions.explanation: The chapter ends by saying you will learn more about these particles (atoms and molecules) in higher grades.

questions.question: In the context of air pollution, 'Suspended Particulate Matter (SPM)' refers to
options: tiny water droplets suspended in clouds
atoms of oxygen and nitrogen in air
tiny dust particles suspended in the air
the constituent particles of the air's gases
questions.explanation: SPM means tiny dust particles suspended in air — not the constituent particles of matter, which are far smaller.

questions.question: Compared with the constituent particles of matter, the dust particles of SPM are
options: about the same size, since both are called particles
far smaller, which is why they can float in the air
not made up of any constituent particles at all
far larger, and themselves made of constituent particles
questions.explanation: The chapter says constituent particles are extremely small compared to dust particles, and even dust particles are made of very many atoms and molecules.

questions.question: The term 'particle' always means the constituent particle of matter, whatever the context.
questions.explanation: 'A step further' notes the meaning of 'particle' changes with context — e.g. SPM dust particles are not constituent particles.

questions.question: When oil-stained clothes are washed with soap, one end of a soap particle attaches to the oil and the other end
options: mixes with water, helping lift the oil off
attaches itself firmly to the fabric fibres
attaches to another nearby oil particle
evaporates away into the surrounding air
questions.explanation: One end of the soap particle attaches to the oil and the other mixes with water, so the oil is lifted off the fabric and washed away.

questions.question: The soap example in 'Ever heard of…' is given to show that
options: soap raises the boiling point of the water used for washing
the particle nature of matter is useful in everyday life
soap is a fluid that takes the shape of its container
oil particles are much larger than water particles
questions.explanation: The box opens by saying the particulate nature of matter plays a crucial role in many everyday processes, with washing as the example.

questions.question: According to 'A step further', the tiny particles that make up all matter are
options: pebbles and stones
cells and tissues
atoms and molecules
sand grains and dust
questions.explanation: The box states that the tiny particles making up all matter are atoms and molecules.

questions.question: According to the chapter, iron is made up of
options: molecules of hydrogen
atoms of gold
particles of rust
atoms of iron
questions.explanation: The chapter gives iron and gold as examples: iron is made of atoms of iron, gold of atoms of gold.

questions.question: Atoms of hydrogen, oxygen and sulfur cannot exist independently. In such cases,
options: atoms of that element combine to form a molecule
the atoms break down into several smaller atoms
the atoms dissolve in water in order to stay stable
the atoms turn into atoms of a different element
questions.explanation: A certain number of atoms of the same element combine to form a molecule — e.g. two hydrogen atoms form a hydrogen molecule.

questions.question: A molecule of hydrogen is formed from
options: one hydrogen and one oxygen atom
two hydrogen atoms
one hydrogen atom
two oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: Two atoms of hydrogen combine to form a stable particle called a molecule of hydrogen.

questions.question: A water molecule is made up of
options: two hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms
one hydrogen atom and one oxygen atom
two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom
one hydrogen atom and two oxygen atoms
questions.explanation: The chapter says a water molecule is made up of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

questions.question: Gold is made up of atoms of gold, and two hydrogen atoms combine to form a stable molecule of hydrogen.
questions.explanation: Both facts are given in 'A step further'.

questions.question: Which statement about atoms and molecules is NOT correct according to the chapter?
options: Iron is made of atoms of iron
A water molecule has two hydrogen atoms
Some atoms combine to form molecules
All atoms can exist independently
questions.explanation: Atoms of many elements like hydrogen, oxygen and sulfur cannot exist independently; they combine to form molecules.

questions.question: Which of these are molecules as described in 'A step further'? (Select all that apply)
options: A hydrogen molecule made of two hydrogen atoms
A water molecule with two hydrogen and one oxygen atom
A gold molecule made of two gold atoms
An iron molecule made of iron and oxygen
questions.explanation: The chapter describes the hydrogen molecule and the water molecule. Gold and iron are described as made of atoms, not molecules.

questions.question: The chapter's speech bubble explains that the fragrance of perfume reaches us because
options: fragrance particles spread as moving air particles hit them
the perfume liquid flows across the floor towards us
perfume particles are attracted towards our noses
perfume turns into solid particles that fall near us
questions.explanation: After the incense activity, the chapter notes this is 'why and how the fragrance of perfume reaches us' — air particles hit fragrance particles and spread them.

questions.question: The primary difference between solids and liquids is that the constituent particles are
options: always moving in solids and have fixed positions in liquids
closely packed in solids and move past each other in liquids
closely packed in solids, while they are stationary in liquids
far apart in solids and have fixed positions in liquids
questions.explanation: Solid particles are closely packed and fixed; liquid particles can move past each other within a limited space. Liquid particles are not stationary.

questions.question: Melting ice into water is an example of the transformation of a solid into a liquid.
questions.explanation: Ice is solid water; melting at 0 °C converts it into liquid water.

questions.question: The melting process involves an increase in interparticle attractions during the transformation.
questions.explanation: Melting involves a DECREASE in interparticle attraction as particles gain energy and move apart. The original exercise statement (decrease) is true.

questions.question: Solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume.
questions.explanation: This is one of the true statements in Exercise 2 and a core property of solids.

questions.question: The interparticle interactions in solids are very strong, and the interparticle spaces are very small.
questions.explanation: Strong attractions and minimum interparticle space are what give solids their fixed shape and volume.

questions.question: When camphor is heated in one corner of a room, its fragrance reaches all corners of the room.
questions.explanation: Heating gives camphor particles energy to escape, and moving air particles spread them throughout the room, just like incense fragrance.

questions.question: Statement: 'On heating, we are adding energy to the camphor, and the energy is released as a smell.' Which correction makes it true?
options: Heating adds no energy; the smell comes from the air particles instead
The energy is released as light, which our noses then sense as smell
The energy makes camphor particles escape and spread in the air; smell is not energy
The energy is stored in the camphor and released later as heat, not as smell
questions.explanation: Heat energy increases particle motion so camphor particles leave and spread through the air; the smell is those particles reaching us, not energy being released.

questions.question: If we could remove all the constituent particles from a chair, what would happen?
options: Nothing about the chair will change
The chair will weigh less but keep its shape
The chair will turn into a liquid
Nothing of the chair will remain
questions.explanation: Matter is composed entirely of its constituent particles, so removing all of them leaves nothing of the chair.

questions.question: The justification for the answer to the chair question (Exercise 3) is that
options: the chair is entirely made up of its constituent particles
particles can be removed without changing the chair
only some of the chair's mass comes from its particles
the chair's shape is held by air, not by particles
questions.explanation: Since all matter is composed of constituent particles, there is nothing else to the chair besides them.

questions.question: Why do gases mix easily while solids do not?
options: Gases are lighter than solids, so they float upward and mix together
Gas particles move freely with negligible attraction; solid particles are held fixed
Gas particles are much smaller than solid particles, so they slip in between each other
Solids have more interparticle space, which traps particles inside them
questions.explanation: Gas particles move freely in all directions with negligible attraction and large spaces, so they intermix; solid particles are held in fixed positions.

questions.question: Spilled milk flows and spreads on a table, but the glass tumbler keeps its shape, because
options: milk particles are far apart like a gas; glass particles are also far apart
milk is a fluid with a fixed shape; glass is a solid with no fixed shape
milk is a liquid with freely moving particles; glass is a solid with fixed particles
milk has negligible interparticle attraction like a gas; glass has only weak attraction
questions.explanation: Liquids have no fixed shape because their particles move; solids keep their shape because strong attraction holds particles in place.

questions.question: As ice melts into water and then turns into water vapour, the arrangement of particles changes from
options: free and far apart → closely packed → a little loosely packed
a little loosely packed → closely packed → free and far apart
closely packed → free and far apart → a little loosely packed
closely packed → a little loosely packed → free and far apart
questions.explanation: Solid → liquid → gas: particles go from closely packed with minimum spacing, to a little more loosely packed, to free with maximum spacing.

questions.question: In a particle picture of aluminium foil and methane gas, the particles should be drawn
options: closely packed for aluminium foil; far apart and free for methane
far apart for aluminium foil; closely packed for methane
a little loosely packed for both, since both are fluids
closely packed for both, since both are made of atoms
questions.explanation: Aluminium foil is a solid (closely packed, minimum spacing); methane is a gas (particles free, maximum spacing).

questions.question: Ocean water tastes salty even though no salt is visible because
options: salt particles are heavy and settle at the bottom of the ocean
salt breaks into tiny particles that fill spaces between water particles
salt floats on the surface as a very thin, invisible layer
salt turns into a gas that then dissolves back into the water
questions.explanation: Like sugar in Activity 7.2, dissolved salt exists as constituent particles too small to see, spread in the interparticle spaces of water — sensed by taste.

questions.question: Grains of rice and rice flour take the shape of the container they are placed in. They are
options: fluids, because they can be poured just like water
gases, because they fill the space available in the jar
solids, because each grain has its own definite shape and volume
liquids, because they flow and take the shape of the container
questions.explanation: Each grain or flour particle is a solid with a fixed shape and volume; only the collection appears to take the container's shape because the pieces are small and loose.

questions.question: Which of these exercise statements are TRUE? (Select all that apply)
options: Solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume
Melting ice into water is a solid-to-liquid transformation
On heating camphor, the energy is released as a smell
Melting increases the interparticle attractions
questions.explanation: The first two are true. Energy is not released as smell (particles spread), and melting decreases, not increases, interparticle attraction.
